en: *The Treatise on the Original Person*, composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cudang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan. 1.
Refuting Deluded Attachments. Part One: Those Who Practice Confucianism and Daoism.
The two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism maintain that all categories of beings, including humans and animals, are generated and nurtured by the Great Way of Non-being (xūwú dàodào).

They assert that according to the Dao, things arise spontaneously from primordial qi (yuánqì); primordial qi gives birth to heaven and earth; and heaven and earth give birth to the myriad things. Therefore, whether one is foolish or wise, noble or humble, poor or wealthy, suffering or happy, all are received from Heaven and depend upon destiny and fate.
Consequently, after death, they return to heaven and earth, restoring themselves to non-being.
However, the fundamental tenets of external teachings consist merely in establishing practice based upon the physical body, rather than investigating the ultimate origin of the body.

Their discourse on the myriad phenomena does not address that which transcends forms; although they point to the Great Way as the source, they do not fully clarify the causes and conditions of accordance and opposition, arising and ceasing, or defilement and purity. Consequently, practitioners fail to recognize these as provisional means and instead cling to them as the final realization.
Now, let me briefly cite these points to challenge you.

As for your claim that all things arise from the Great Way of Non-being (xūwú dàodào), this Great Way is the very root of birth and death, of the wise and the foolish, and the foundation of good fortune and misfortune, of calamity and blessing.

If the fundamental were eternally constant, then calamity, disorder, wickedness, and folly could not be eliminated, nor could fortune, celebration, worthiness, and goodness be increased; what, then, would be the use of the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi?

Furthermore, if [the Way] nourishes tigers and wolves and brings forth Jie and Zhou from the womb; if it shortens the lives of Yan Hui and Ran Geng and brings calamity upon Yi Yin and Zhongni—how can it be called "honorable"?

Moreover, if you claim that all things arise through spontaneous transformation (*ziran shenghua*) rather than through causes and conditions (*yinyuan*), then everything that lacks causes and conditions should likewise undergo such transformation: stones should produce grass, grass might produce humans, and humans should produce livestock and so forth.

Furthermore, birth would have no sequence of before and after, and arising would have no distinction of early or late; immortals would not rely on elixirs and medicines, the Great Peace would not rely on worthy and good men, and benevolence and righteousness would not rely on instruction and practice—then what purpose would Laozi, Zhuangzi, Confucius, and Zhou Gong have served in establishing teachings as rules?

Furthermore, regarding the claim that all things are generated from the primal qi (yuanqi), if the spirit that suddenly arises has never undergone training or reflection, how could an infant immediately possess likes and dislikes, as well as arrogance and indulgence?

If one were to claim that things arise suddenly and spontaneously such that one can immediately follow one's thoughts regarding likes and dislikes and so forth, then one would likewise be able to understand the five virtues and six arts instantly upon thought; why then wait for them to be accomplished through the causes and conditions of study and training?

Furthermore, if birth were merely the sudden existence resulting from receiving vital energy (*qi*), and death were merely the sudden non-existence resulting from the dispersal of that energy, then who would constitute ghosts and spirits?

Moreover, there are those in the world who possess insight into past lives and can recall former events; thus we know that before birth there was a continuity of existence, rather than a sudden coming into being through the reception of *qi*.
Furthermore, by verifying that the spiritual consciousness of ghosts and spirits is uninterrupted, we know that after death there is not a sudden non-existence due to the dispersal of *qi*.

Therefore, performing sacrifices and seeking prayers through them is attested by the texts of the classics; how much more so when those who have died and returned to life speak of matters from the dark paths, or when, after death, they move their wives and children to seek vengeance for grievances or repay kindnesses—such things have occurred throughout both ancient and modern times, have they not?
An external critic objects:
"If when a person dies they become a ghost, then the ghosts from all ages since antiquity would fill the streets and alleys; there ought to be those who see them.
Why is this not the case?"
He replied:

"When humans die, they enter one of the six realms; it is not necessarily that they all become ghosts. When ghosts die, they are reborn as humans and so forth; how could it be that the ghosts accumulated since antiquity exist eternally?"
Furthermore, the qi of heaven and earth is fundamentally without consciousness; since humans receive this unconscious qi, how could it suddenly arise and possess consciousness?
Grasses and trees also all receive qi; why are they not conscious?

Furthermore, as for the claim that poverty and wealth, nobility and lowliness, wisdom and folly, good and evil, and fortune or misfortune, calamity and blessing, all arise from the mandate of Heaven: if this were so, why would Heaven’s allotment of mandates consist of so much poverty and so little wealth, so much lowliness and so little nobility, and even so much calamity and so little blessing?
If the distinction between much and little is determined by Heaven, why is Heaven not impartial?

Moreover, there are those who lack virtuous conduct yet are honored, while those who maintain such conduct are held in low esteem; those without virtue are wealthy, while those with virtue are poor; the perverse are auspicious and the righteous are ill-fated; the benevolent die young while the violent live long; and even those who possess the Way perish, while those who lack the Way flourish. How can this be?
Since all things depend on Heaven, why does Heaven promote the unrighteous and cause the Way to perish?
Why are there rewards for those who possess blessings, do good, and increase in humility, yet punishments for those who indulge in excess, commit depravity, and become arrogant?

Furthermore, if calamities, rebellions, and acts of defiance all arise from the mandate of Heaven, then it would be improper for the sages to establish their teachings by holding people accountable rather than Heaven, and blaming things rather than the mandate.

That being so, the *Shi* satirizes chaotic governance, the *Shu* extols the Way of the King, the *Li* praises the stability of superiors, and the *Yue* is said to transform customs; how could these be considered acts of serving the will of Heaven above or following the mind of cosmic transformation?
Thus we know that those who specialize solely in these teachings have not yet reached the fundamental understanding of the person. **2.

Refuting Partiality and Superficiality, Part Two.** Those who practice the Buddha’s teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) find that Buddhism proceeds from the shallow to the profound, comprising approximately five levels:

1. The Teaching for Humans and Devas; 2. The Teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*); 3. The Teaching of the Characteristics of Mahāyāna (*Lakṣaṇayāna*); 4. The Teaching of the Destruction of Characteristics (*Dharmatā-yāna*); The first four of these are contained within this present section. 5. The Teaching of the Manifestation of Nature (*Ekayāna-svabhāva-vyakti-yāna*); This fifth level is found in the third section.

First, for beginners, the Buddha provisionally taught the retribution of karma across the three periods of time and the causes and effects of good and evil: namely, that those who commit the ten unwholesome acts of the highest grade will fall into hell after death; those of the middle grade will become hungry ghosts; and those of the lowest grade will become animals.

Therefore, the Buddha’s teachings may be compared to the Five Constant Virtues of the worldly tradition in India; although their ritual forms differ, there is no distinction in their aim to punish evil and encourage good, nor do they depart from benevolence, righteousness, and the other Five Constants, such that there are analogous practices for cultivating virtuous conduct.
For example:

in this country, one raises the hands with palms joined, whereas in Tibet, one lets them hang loosely; both are considered forms of propriety. Furthermore, to observe the five precepts—refraining from killing is benevolence (*ren*);
refraining from stealing is righteousness (*yi*).
Abstaining from sexual misconduct is propriety;
abstaining from false speech is faith;
abstaining from drinking wine and eating meat purifies the spirit and augments wisdom, enabling one to escape the three miserable realms and be reborn among human beings.
By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action in their superior degree, as well as generosity, morality, and so forth, one is reborn in the heavens of the six desire realms (*kāmadhātu*).

By practicing the four dhyānas and eight meditative attainments, one is reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As for the fact that the heavens, ghosts, and hells are not explicitly mentioned in the title, it is because their realms and lands differ; they are beyond the reach of sight and hearing. If even ordinary people do not know the branches, how could they be expected to exhaustively fathom the root?
Therefore, in contrast to worldly teachings, I have provisionally set forth the "Original Person.
Now, as I expound the Buddhist scriptures, it is logically appropriate to provide a complete enumeration;
thus, this is termed the "Teaching for Humans and Gods" (Śrāvakayāna). Furthermore, karma is of three kinds:
There are three types: the unwholesome, the wholesome, and the imperturbable.
There are three times for their retribution:
namely, retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, and retribution in subsequent lives.
According to these teachings, karma is the fundamental basis of the body.
Now, let us interrogate this point:
since one receives a body within the five realms of existence by virtue of having created karma, it remains to be determined who creates the karma and who receives the retribution.

If it were these eyes, ears, hands, and feet that could perform actions, then since the eyes, ears, hands, and feet of a person who has just died remain perfectly intact, why do they not see, hear, or act?
If you say it is the mind that acts, what is this "mind"?

If you say it is the physical heart, the physical heart has substance and is bound within the body; how then could it enter the eyes and ears so swiftly to discern right and wrong in the external world?
Without knowing right from wrong, on what basis could one choose between acceptance and rejection?

Furthermore, since the mind and the eyes, ears, hands, and feet are all characterized by material obstruction, how could they mutually communicate internally to coordinate movement, respond to stimuli, and collectively create karmic conditions?

If you claim that it is merely the arousal of joy, anger, love, or hatred that incites the body and speech to perform actions, then these emotions—joy, anger, and so forth—arise and perish in an instant; having no inherent substance of their own, what could serve as the sovereign agent to perform karma?

If one were to say that this is not the case, and that it is this very body and mind of mine, when investigated individually, that are the agents of action, then once this body has died, who is it that experiences the retribution of pleasure and pain?

If one were to say that there is another body after death, how could the body and mind of today create evil or cultivate merit, thereby causing the body and mind of a future life to experience suffering or joy?
According to this, those who cultivate merit are greatly disadvantaged, while those who commit transgressions are greatly favored; how can the divine principle be so devoid of righteousness?
Thus we know that those who merely study these teachings, though they believe in karmic conditions, do not comprehend the fundamental nature of the body.

Second, as for the teachings of the Hīnayāna: they maintain that the physical form and the thinking mind have, from time immemorial, arisen and ceased moment by moment in an endless succession due to the power of causes and conditions.
Like a trickling stream or a flickering flame, the body and mind are a provisional union that appears to be one and constant; the ignorant and foolish fail to perceive this and grasp it as a self.

Because they treasure this "self," the three poisons arise: greed for fame and profit to glorify the self, hatred toward objects that oppose the self out of fear of harm, and delusion consisting of irrational calculations and the like.
The three poisons strike the mind, inciting the body and speech to create all manner of karma.

Once karma is formed, it is difficult to escape; thus, one undergoes the bodies of suffering and pleasure in the five destinies, which are induced by individual karma, as well as the superior and inferior locations within the triple world, which are induced by collective karma.
Regarding the body one has received, one again clings to it as a self, giving rise once more to craving and other afflictions, thereby creating karma and undergoing retribution.
Thus the body undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; having died, it is born again.
The realms undergo formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; after becoming empty, they form again from the beginning of the kalpa of emptiness. A verse says:
From the great wind arising in the realm of emptiness, Its breadth is immeasurable, And its thickness is sixteen lakṣas, Which even a vajra cannot destroy.
This is called the Wind that Sustains the Realm.

The clouds of the Radiant Sound and Golden Treasury spread throughout the trichiliocosm; rain falls like chariot axles, yet the wind obstructs it so that it does not flow, reaching a depth of eleven lakṣas, whereupon the Vajra-realm first comes into being.
Successively, clouds of golden storehouses pour down rain that fills their interior; first the realm of the Brahma Kings is formed, extending even to the Yāma Heaven.

Driven by winds, clear water forms Mount Sumeru and the seven golden mountains; the turbid dregs become the mountain ranges and the earth, including the four continents and the hells, the salt ocean, and the outer Cakravāḍa mountains—only then is the receptacle world said to be established.
When one cycle of increase and decrease has passed, and even the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted, they descend to be born among humans.

Initially, they subsist on earth-cakes and forest vines; later, when they can no longer digest non-glutinous rice, they experience excrement and urine, and the physical distinctions between male and female emerge. They then divide the fields, establish rulers, and seek ministers and assistants, giving rise to all manner of social distinctions.

Including the nineteen cycles of increase and decrease, together with the preceding [period], they constitute a total of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, which is termed the *vivartakalpa* (the kalpa of formation).
The commentary states:

Within the kalpa of the empty realm (*ākāśadhātu*), this refers to what the Daoist teachings call the Way of Non-being (*xuwu*). However, the essence of the Way is quiescent illumination and spiritual penetration; it is not non-being. Perhaps Laozi was confused by this, or perhaps he established it as a provisional teaching; his aim was to sever human desires, and thus he pointed to the empty realm as the Way.
The great wind within the realm of emptiness is precisely that primordial chaotic breath; thus it is said that "the Dao gives birth to One.
The "clouds stored in gold" represent the beginning of the formation of qi and form; they are the Great Ultimate (Taiji).
When rain falls but does not flow, it is because the yin energy has coagulated.
Only when yin and yang unite can generation and growth occur!
That which extends from the realm of Brahmā down to Mount Sumeru is the celestial; that which is turbid and sedimentary is the terrestrial—this is how the One gives rise to the Two!
When the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted and one is reborn below, this refers to human beings.
Thus, from two comes three, and the Three Powers (Sancai) are complete!
From the "earth-cakes" (dibing) downward, through all various forms of existence, this refers to the third generation of the myriad things.

This refers to the period prior to the Three Sovereigns, when people lived in caves and ate wild foods, and the practice of transforming wood into fire had not yet emerged. However, because there were no written records at that time, later generations have transmitted these accounts unclearly, leading to successive errors and the various divergent theories found in the works of different scholars.

Furthermore, Buddhism extends its scope to illuminate the three thousandfold world system rather than being restricted to the Great Tang; therefore, the texts of the inner and outer teachings are not entirely identical.
As for "abiding," it refers to the kalpa of abiding, which likewise undergoes twenty cycles of increase and decrease.

As for "destruction," this refers to the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), which likewise consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease. During the first nineteen cycles of increase and decrease, sentient beings are destroyed; during the final cycle of increase and decrease, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is destroyed. That which is capable of destroying it consists of the three calamities: fire, water, and wind.

The "void" refers to the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kalpa*), which likewise consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease; during this intermediate void, there are no worlds nor sentient beings.

Kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, the cycle of *saṃsāra* continues without interruption, having neither end nor beginning, like the wheel of a well-drawing mechanism. In Daoism, one only knows that when this present world had not yet been formed, there was once a kalpa of emptiness, described as "void and non-being," "chaotic primordiality," or "the single vital energy" (*yīqì*), which is termed the "Original Beginning" (*yuánshǐ*).

One does not realize that prior to this present empty realm, one has already undergone thousands upon ten thousands of times of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, ending only to begin again.

Therefore, one knows that within the teachings of Buddhism, even the shallow doctrines of the Hinayana surpass the profound assertions of external scriptures; this is entirely because one fails to understand that this body is fundamentally not the self. That it is not the self means that this body originally arises from the conjunction of form and mind as its characteristic.

Now, through investigation and analysis, one finds that form consists of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind; while mind consists of the four aggregates: sensation (*vedanā*), which is capable of experiencing pleasant and unpleasant matters; perception (*saṃjñā*), which is capable of grasping images; formations (*saṃskāra*), which are capable of creating and flow on from moment to moment; and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is capable of discerning.
If all these were the self, there would already be eight selves; how much more so since within the earth element there are many more?
That is to say, there are three hundred and sixty pieces of bone, each of which is distinct.
The skin, hair, muscles, liver, heart, spleen, and kidneys are each distinct from one another;
likewise, the various mental factors (*caitasika*) are each different.
What is seen is not what is heard; joy is not anger; and so it continues in succession through the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since there are already so many such things, one does not know which among them should definitively be taken as the self.
If all of them were the self, then there would be hundreds or thousands of selves;
within a single body, there would be the chaos of many masters.
Apart from this, there is no other separate phenomenon.
Whether one turns it over or examines it from every angle, the "self" cannot be found.

Thus, one realizes that this body is merely a collection of conditions, appearing as a composite of signs; fundamentally, there is neither self nor person. For whom, then, would there be greed or anger?
For whom does the truth of suffering consist in the knowledge of killing, stealing, giving, and precepts?
Consequently, one does not allow the mind to stagnate in the outflows of the three realms of existence, thereby severing the truth of origination;
one merely cultivates the wisdom of the path, which is the contemplation of non-self.
By severing greed and the other afflictions, one brings all karma to rest;

by realizing the *tathatā* (suchness) of the truth of cessation—the emptiness of self—one attains the fruit of arhatship, whereupon the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished, finally severing all suffering.

According to this school, the two dharmas of form and mind, along with greed, hatred, and delusion, constitute the basis of the root-body and the vessel-world; there are no other distinct dharmas that serve as the basis for the past or the future.
Now, let us interrogate this: that which serves as the fundamental basis for the body throughout successive lifetimes must, by its very nature, exist without interruption.

Yet, the five consciousnesses fail to arise when conditions are lacking; the sense organs and objects serve as their conditions, yet there are times when the mental consciousness does not function—such as during fainting, sleep, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), or in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*). Furthermore, in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), these four great elements do not exist. How, then, could they sustain this body so that it remains unbroken from lifetime to lifetime?
Thus we know that those who focus solely on this teaching have likewise not yet investigated the nature of the self.
Third, the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa Teaching states that all sentient beings have, from time immemorial, naturally possessed eight kinds of consciousness.

Among these, the eighth ālayavijñāna is the fundamental basis; it suddenly transforms the seeds of the sense organs, the body, and the environmental world, giving rise to the seven evolving consciousnesses, all of which can manifest their own respective objects, none of which possess any real dharmas.
How does this transformation occur?

It is said that due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination between self and phenomena, when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as if they were a self and phenomena. Because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*), they take these appearances as objects and cling to them as a real self and real phenomena.

For example, when one suffers from a grave illness and the mind is clouded, one may see various forms, people, and objects, or perceive what was seen in dreams. This is due to the power of the illness and the dreaming state; various external objective appearances manifest to the mind, and during the dream, one clings to them as if they were real external things. Only upon waking does one realize that these were merely transformations of the dream.

My body is likewise so: it is a transformation of consciousness alone; due to delusion, one clings to the existence of a self and various objects, and from this, one gives rise to afflictions and creates karma, resulting in an endless cycle of birth and death, as explained at length previously.

Only upon awakening to this principle does one come to know that one’s own body is a transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), and that consciousness is the fundamental basis of the body—a point not yet understood, as will be refuted later.

Fourth, the Mahāyāna Teaching on the Refutation of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vināśana*) refutes the attachments to the phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna vehicles, while secretly revealing the subsequent principle of the true nature’s emptiness and quiescence. This discourse on the refutation of characteristics is found not only in the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, but pervades all Mahāyāna scriptures.
The first three teachings follow a fixed sequence of priority, whereas this teaching refutes attachments as they arise, without a fixed temporal order.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna established two kinds of Prajñā:
the common and the uncommon.
The "shared" [teaching] is that which is heard, believed, and understood by both vehicles alike, for it destroys the attachment to the teachings of the two vehicles.
The "unshared" [teaching] is that which is understood only by bodhisattvas, for it secretly reveals the Buddha-nature.

Therefore, the two Indian masters Śīlabhadra and Jñānaprabha each established a system of the three-period teachings; regarding this teaching of emptiness, one held it to precede the Vijñaptimātra-dharmalakṣaṇa teachings, while the other held it to follow them.
Now, we shall adopt the latter view.
Being about to refute it, we first challenge it by asking:
"If the objects that undergo transformation are illusory, how can the consciousness that performs the transformation be real?"

If one claims that [the dream object] both exists and does not exist, this section below refutes that claim using the analogy itself: the dream-illusion and the perceived object should then be distinct. If they were distinct, the dream would not be the object, and the object would not be the dream.
When one awakens and the dream ceases, the object [of the dream] should still exist.
Furthermore, if the object were not a dream, it would have to be a real thing;
if the dream were not a thing, by what means could it possess characteristics?

Therefore, we know that during a dream, one conceives of dreams and dream-objects; while these appear as a distinction between the seer and the seen, according to the principle, they are equally empty and false, being entirely non-existent.
The various consciousnesses are likewise so, for they all depend upon a multitude of conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions;
therefore, there is no phenomenon that is not empty."
Furthermore, it is said: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "All dharmas exist only through the distinctions of deluded thought; if one is free from mental conceptions, then there are no appearances of any objective realms whatsoever."
The Sūtra states: "Whatever has marks is all false and illusory; to be free from all marks is itself called the Buddhas. Passages such as these abound throughout the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.
Thus we know that when both mind and objects are empty, this alone constitutes the true principle of the Mahāyāna.
If we consider this original body, the body is fundamentally empty, and emptiness is its very source.
Now, let us further interrogate this teaching:
if both mind and objects are non-existent, who is it that knows their non-existence?
Furthermore, if there were no real dharmas whatsoever, upon what could these various delusions depend for their manifestation?
Moreover, we observe in the world that no delusory thing ever arises without depending upon a real dharma.
Just as there can be no waves of false and provisional appearance without water that is unchanging in its lack of moisture,
how could there be various false and provisional reflections without a mirror that is pure, luminous, and unchanging?
Furthermore, as for the previous statement that dreams and dream-objects are equally illusory, it is indeed as you have said;
however, this illusory dream must necessarily depend upon a person who is asleep.
Now that both mind and objects are seen to be empty, I do not yet understand upon what basis these delusive appearances manifest.
Therefore, I know that this teaching merely destroys clinging attachments; it has also not yet clearly revealed the nature of the true spirit.
Therefore, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* states: "All sūtras on emptiness are 'with remainder' (sāvaśeṣa); 'with remainder' means that further meanings remain unclarified.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Emptiness is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna."
These four preceding teachings, when viewed in relation to one another, progress from the shallow to the profound.
If one practices them and realizes for oneself that they are not yet fully understood, they are termed "shallow";
if one clings to them as being complete, they are termed "partial."
Therefore, according to those who follow conventional learning, it is said that [this teaching] is partial and shallow.

**3. Directly Revealing the True Source.** **Section Three: The Buddha’s Teaching of the Definitive and Ultimate Meaning.** **V. The Teaching of the One Vehicle that Reveals Nature:** This teaches that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*—the true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*). Since beginningless time, it has remained eternally abiding and pure; it is luminously clear and never obscured, being ever-present and fully cognizant. It is also called "Buddha-nature" and "Tathāgata-garbha."

Since beginningless time, they have been obscured by delusive appearances and have failed to realize this for themselves; merely identifying with their ordinary physical substance, they become attached to the karma of their fetters and undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Out of compassion for them, the Great Awakened One taught that all things are empty, and further revealed that the true mind of numinous awareness is pure and identical in every respect to that of the Buddhas.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it."
If one is free from deluded thoughts, all-knowing wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, and unimpeded wisdom will immediately manifest before them.

He then offers the analogy of a single mote of dust containing a great thousand-fold world-system scripture: the mote of dust represents sentient beings, and the scripture represents the Buddha’s wisdom.
Subsequently, it further states: At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed the entire realm of phenomena and all sentient beings, and spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!
These sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet how is it that they are deluded and do not perceive it?"

I shall instruct them in the Noble Path so that they may forever be free from delusive thoughts, and within their own bodies realize the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is no different from that of the Buddha.

The commentary states: For many kalpas, we have not encountered the True Dharma; failing to understand how to return to our original source, we merely cling to illusory appearances and willingly identify ourselves as ordinary beings—whether as animals or as humans.

Now, by tracing this back to the ultimate teaching, one realizes for the first time that one is originally a Buddha; therefore, one must practice in accordance with the Buddha’s conduct and align the mind with the Buddha’s mind.

Returning to the root and restoring the source, one cuts off mundane habits, diminishing them again and again until reaching the state of non-action (*wuwei*); thus, the natural application of wisdom becomes as vast as the sands of the Ganges, and this is what is called "Buddha."

One should know that delusion and enlightenment are of one and the same true mind. How magnificent is this wondrous gate! When tracing the origin of man to this point, the Buddha taught the first five teachings—whether gradual or sudden; for those with middling or inferior capacities, he led them from the shallow to the profound, gradually guiding and receiving them.
First, the initial teaching is expounded to cause one to leave evil and abide in goodness;
next, the second and third teachings are expounded to cause one to leave defilement and abide in purity;

finally, the fourth and fifth teachings are expounded to shatter appearances and reveal the nature, to bring provisional means back to the ultimate reality, and to cultivate according to the teaching of reality until the attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding those of the highest and most superior faculties, from the beginning to the end, it means that from the outset they rely on the fifth [teaching], which directly points to the essence of the single true mind. Once the essence of the mind is revealed, they realize for themselves that all things are entirely illusory and originally empty and quiescent; it is only due to delusion that they rely upon the Truth and give rise to [the phenomenal world].

One must employ the wisdom that awakens to truth to sever evil and cultivate goodness; by cultivating goodness, one quiets delusion and returns to truth. When delusion is exhausted and truth is perfected, this is called the Dharmakāya Buddha.

4. Synthesizing the Fundamental and the Derivative. This fourth section synthesizes what was previously refuted, showing that all things return to a single source. While the True Nature is indeed the fundamental basis of the body, its arising must have a causal origin; it cannot suddenly manifest as the form of a body without cause.
However, because the preceding thesis was not yet fully understood, it was refuted point by point.

Now, I shall synthesize the beginning and the end: even Confucianism and Daoism initially belong only to the teachings of the fifth nature; from the subsequent sections onward, they gradually align with the various other teachings, each as explained in the commentary.
This refers to the initial state of the single, true spiritual nature, which is neither born nor extinguished, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither changing nor altering.
Sentient beings have been mired in beginningless delusion and sleep, failing to realize it for themselves; because it is obscured and concealed, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Based upon this *tathāgatagarbha*, the characteristics of the mind of birth and extinction arise from this point onward—this constitutes the Fourth Teaching—and likewise, once this has been refuted, all such characteristics of birth and extinction are eliminated.

The so-called true mind, which is neither born nor extinguished, and its deluded thoughts, which are subject to birth and extinction, are in a state of union that is neither identical nor distinct; this is termed the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

This consciousness possesses two aspects: awareness and non-awareness. This point is precisely what is taught here, and it is likewise explained within the third category of the Dharma-characteristics teachings (*lakṣaṇa-śāsana*).
Based on non-awakening, the initial movement of thought is called the "phase of karma.

Furthermore, because one does not awaken to the fact that this thought is fundamentally non-existent, it transforms into the consciousness that perceives and the manifestation of the objective realm that is perceived.

Furthermore, failing to realize that this object is a false manifestation from one's own mind and instead grasping it as truly existent is termed "clinging to phenomena" (dharmagrāha). This point is exactly what is taught in the second category, the Hīnayāna teachings.
Because one clings to these [notions], one perceives the distinction between self and other, whereby self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) arises.
Clinging to the mark of a self, one craves those objects that accord with one's desires in order to nourish this self;
one feels aversion toward those objects that conflict with one's desires, fearing they will cause harm or affliction.
The emotions of ignorance increase and proliferate one after another; this is what is likewise taught in the first of the teachings for humans and devas.
Thus, through these evil karmas, the mind and spirit ride upon them to be born among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth.

Furthermore, there are those who fear this suffering, or those who are virtuous by nature; through the mental continuum of practicing generosity, observing precepts, and so forth, they ride upon these wholesome karmas to transport themselves into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and enter the mother’s womb. This point is likewise taught in both the Confucian and Daoist traditions.

Regarding the reception of vital energy (*prāṇa*) and the acquisition of physical substance (*bhūta*), as explained in other teachings, energy is taken as the fundamental basis; thus, energy is instantaneously endowed with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which gradually form the various sense organs (*indriya*). Likewise, the mind is instantaneously endowed with the four aggregates (*skandha*), which gradually form the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
When ten months have been fulfilled, one is born and called a "human being"; this refers precisely to our present body and mind.
Thus we know that the body and mind each have their own source, and only through the conjunction of these two categories does a single person come to be formed.
The same applies generally to the devas, asuras, and others.

Although this body is acquired through the drawing power of *ākṣepaka-karman* (projecting karma), it is further by virtue of *paripūrakak-karman* (fulfilling karma) that there arise distinctions of noble and lowly, rich and poor, long life and early death, health and sickness, prosperity and decline, and suffering and happiness.
This means that with respect and pride in previous lives serving as causes, one now experiences the fruits of nobility or lowliness.

This extends even to longevity versus premature death through benevolence or killing, wealth through giving versus poverty through stinginess; such various distinct retributions cannot be described in full detail.

Therefore, when there are cases where this body experiences misfortune despite the absence of evil, or fortune despite the absence of merit; or where one lives long despite being unkind, or dies young despite not killing—these are all because the full karma (*pūrṇakarma*) from previous lives has already been fixed. Consequently, differences in the present life occur naturally as such. Those of external schools do not know of past lives and rely solely on what is visible to the eye; they cling only to "naturalness" (*svabhāva*) to interpret those teachings, taking naturalness as the fundamental principle.
Furthermore, there are those who practiced virtue in their youth but committed evil in their old age;
or those who were evil in their youth but virtuous in their old age. Consequently, some are wealthy, noble, and happy in their youth but poor, lowly, and suffering in their old age;
while others are poor and suffering in their youth but wealthy and noble in their old age, and so forth.

Therefore, those who study outside [this tradition] do not understand this; they merely cling to the idea that prosperity and decline depend on the movements of fortune, asserting that all such things are due to the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*).
However, if one traces back the vital energy (*qi*) one has received through successive stages, it is none other than the primordial, unified *yuanqi*;
and if one exhaustively seeks the source of the mind that arises, it is none other than the true, singular spiritual mind.
To speak of the ultimate reality, there are no phenomena distinct from the mind.

Even the primal vital energy (qi) arises from the transformations of the mind; it belongs to the objects manifested by the preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and is subsumed within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

From the first thought-moment of karmic appearance (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), it divides into the duality of mind and object. As the mind proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, it undergoes successive false conceptualizations until the performance of karma as previously enumerated;

the object likewise proceeds from the minute to the manifest, undergoing successive transformations until the heavens and earth arise—beginning from that primordial state of *taiyi*, through five stages of evolution up to *taiji*, and from *taiji* the two polarities (*liangyi*) are produced.

They speak of the Great Way of spontaneity (*ziran*) and describe it as suchness (*tathatā*); in reality, however, it is merely the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that undergoes transformation within a single thought-moment.
They say that the primal qi (*yuánqì*) is thus the initial movement of this single thought-moment.
In reality, these are merely the marks of objective realms.
Once karma has matured, one receives the two vital energies from the parents; through their union with the karmic consciousness, a human body is formed.
Based on this, the objects transformed by the mind-consciousness constitute two portions.

One portion is conjoined with the mind-consciousness to form the person; the other portion is not conjoined with the mind-consciousness, forming the heavens, earth, mountains, rivers, nations, and towns.
That among the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) only humanity is spiritual is because it is united with the mind and spirit.
That the Buddha taught the internal four elements are different from the external four elements is precisely this point.
How lamentable!

Those with meager learning hold diverse and chaotic attachments. I address those in the Way who wish to attain Buddhahood: you must thoroughly clarify both the coarse and the subtle, as well as the root and the branches; only then can you abandon the branches to return to the root and reflect back upon the source of the mind.
When the coarse is exhausted and the subtle is eliminated, the numinous nature manifests; reaching all phenomena without exception, it is called the Dharmakāya (Dharma-Body);
manifesting endlessly in response to conditions, it is called the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha (Transformation-Body Buddha).
The Treatise on the Primordial Person concludes.
